review: Kantor Gottfried (a church musician in Leipzig, 1735): I am pleased that the phrases close properly, with honest cadences; the voices move with propriety; the melody sits squarely on the beat. The melody is quite memorable – I find myself humming it.

layers.text: Only the skeleton of the tune is kept (its strong-beat notes). The notes in between are re-composed as classical scale passages.
The bass is re-written as a period bass line (walking, Alberti or sustained).
The original backing is replaced by the composer's own accompaniment textures over (re-)harmonised chords.
No drums. The rhythm comes from the accompaniment, as in real classical music.

era.name: Baroque
era.summary: Music built from interweaving lines (counterpoint) over a constantly moving bass, with ornamented melodies and steady, motor-like rhythm.
traits: Counterpoint: several independent melodic lines at once
Basso continuo: a bass line plus harpsichord filling in the chords
Terraced dynamics: whole sections loud or soft, rarely gradual
Ornaments: trills, mordents and decorated long notes
One steady pulse and mood per movement
era.instruments: Strings, harpsichord, organ, recorder/flute, oboe, bassoon, natural trumpet, timpani
why: All three eras were tried. Baroque scored best (Baroque 1.047, Romantic 1.022, Classical 1.002). The score combines how classical it sounds, how much of the song survives, and how well the song suits the composer.
The vocal line mostly sits on the beat, so it survives Baroque's strict pulse with little change.
The energy stays fairly even from verse to chorus, matching Baroque's one-mood-per-piece style.

composer.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
composer.bio: The great master of counterpoint: several melodies woven together over a walking bass, every line meaningful.
reasons: its fairly even energy suits a steady, unbroken style
applied: A walking continuo bass moves under every beat
Terraced dynamics: whole sections are loud or soft, Baroque-style
Re-harmonised more freely toward the composer's harmonic language

top.name: Bach
reasons: its fairly even energy suits a steady, unbroken style

ensemble.name: Chamber ensemble
ensemble.summary: A wind soloist with strings (and keyboard): flute for Baroque and Classical styles, clarinet for Romantic ones.
why: It is one of Bach's favourite settings.
In this composer's style it scored best of the four ensembles: Chamber ensemble 1.047, Solo keyboard 0.987, String quartet 0.976, Orchestra 0.959.
Why it works: a contrasting wind colour on the melody makes the tune stand out from the strings.
The flute carries the vocal melody (E5–F6). It was moved by octaves into the instrument's most singing register, with the key unchanged.

parts.what: A wind soloist (flute or clarinet) carries the tune
Doubles the line above for extra weight and colour

changes.ending: It follows the original beat by beat and lasts exactly as long as the clip (19.3s).
changes.dropped: The drum kit, synths and electric bass are gone. Their rhythmic drive now comes from the accompaniment patterns.
